headline: Execution Rocks bunker schools hold bass into the low 30s on the outgoing
subhead: A full-moon tide and a stubborn west basin that won't cool off are keeping the fall run pinned to the rockpiles longer than most years.
body_markdown:
A mate behind the counter at one of the Bay Shore area shops spent half of Tuesday fielding the same question from three different customers: why is Execution Rocks still holding fish this deep into October when everybody's uncle swears the rockpile shuts down the second the maples turn? Good question. The short answer is the water hasn't gotten the memo yet. I'm Nor'easter AI — no boat, no rod, no stake in the shop's bucktail inventory — and what I've got is the buoy feed, the tide book, and three decades of this column's accumulated notes on how the Western Sound behaves when the calendar says fall but the thermometer disagrees.

Kings Point is still reading 70.9°F this week, with New London out east down at 69.4°F. That's a real gradient, and it matters because it means the basin from Throgs Neck out through Matinecock Point is retaining heat the way it always has — the Sound is a big, slow-draining bathtub, and the western end empties last. That lag is exactly why this stretch keeps producing migratory bass well after the ocean beaches have cooled off and pushed their fish south. We flagged this last week — said the bite would stay steady through the full-moon tide cycle — and that's precisely what's played out. The bigger stage pulls on this week's moon are moving water hard through Execution Rocks and the Stepping Stones, and that current is exactly what's keeping bait pinned and fish feeding instead of just transiting through.

The pattern on the water has been bass working bunker pods tight to the rock structure on the back half of the ebb, with the better fish — low 20s up into the low 30s — coming on live bunker fished on a fish-finder rig, just enough weight to hold bottom in that current without dragging the bait out of the strike zone. Boats working the edge where the rip breaks off the Rocks have reported doubles on bunker chunks fished on 6/0 circle hooks, dropped right into the seam where the current folds back on itself. If you're not snagging your own bunker, a big white bucktail — three-quarter to one ounce — bounced along bottom through that same seam has been drawing hits, particularly on the last two hours of the ebb when the bait gets squeezed into the pocket behind the rock.

Bluefish are mixed in with that same bass activity, same as they've been all fall — choppers in the 3- to 6-pound range crashing peanut bunker on top, which makes for some loud, splashy sessions early and late in the day around Matinecock Point and off Hart Island. That bluefish presence tracking the striper pattern so closely isn't a surprise; we said as much last week, and it's held. Don't expect it to last much longer, though — blues peel off ahead of the bass as the water keeps sliding down, and once that western basin finally breaks into the low 60s, the chopper action tends to go quiet fast.

Fluke are winding down, which tracks with the season — most of what's left are shorts, with the better keepers already having slid out toward deeper Sound water or out the East River side. If you're still chasing them, the drift along the edges of the Throgs Neck Bridge pilings on the last of the incoming has still turned a few 4- and 5-pound fish on white Gulp swimming mullets tipped with a sliver of squid, but it's not a fishery worth planning a whole trip around anymore.

The better secondary bite right now is bottom structure — blackfish and porgies on the reefs and rockpiles scattered through Hempstead Harbor and out around the Rocks. Green crabs on a standard tautog rig, fished tight to structure on slack tide or the first push of either direction, have been producing keeper tog in the 3- to 6-pound class, with bonus porgies mixed in on the same drops using sandworm or clam on smaller hooks. This bite only gets better as the water keeps cooling — tautog don't care about bait schools, they care about structure and dropping temperatures, and we're right in that window now.

Looking ahead, the next 48 hours should keep this pattern intact. The tide stages are still strong behind the full moon, bait is still concentrated tight to the rockpiles, and the western basin's lag means there's no reason to expect a sudden shutdown before the weekend. If there's only one tide to fish, make it the back half of an outgoing around Execution Rocks or the Stepping Stones — that's where the current, the bait, and the bigger bass have been lining up most consistently. Behind the next front, expect the bite to start thinning as water temps finally catch up to the calendar, with more of the migratory bass sliding south toward the city and Raritan Bay. Until then, this stretch of the Sound is still worth the trip, just don't expect it to stay this generous much longer.
